content: Acute viral nasopharyngitis, commonly referred to as the common cold, is a highly contagious viral infection of the upper respiratory tract. It is most frequently caused by rhinoviruses, though other viruses such as coronaviruses and picornaviruses can also be responsible. The condition is characterized by symptoms such as a sore throat, runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing, and coughing. Additional symptoms may include muscle aches, fatigue, malaise, headache, muscle weakness, or loss of appetite. Fever and severe exhaustion are more typical of influenza rather than the common cold. Symptoms generally resolve within one week but can persist for up to 14 days, with infants and young children often experiencing more severe manifestations. Although the common cold is typically mild and self-limiting, it leads to significant societal and economic burdens, including missed school or workdays and frequent medical consultations. In the United States alone, the annual societal cost of the common cold amounts to billions of dollars. There are currently no vaccines available to prevent the common cold, and no antiviral drugs have been approved to treat or cure the infection. Most treatments are symptomatic, focusing on alleviating discomfort rather than addressing the underlying viral infection. While megadoses of vitamin C, echinacea preparations, and zinc gluconate have been studied as potential treatments, none have received approval from regulatory agencies such as the FDA or EMA. Historically, the common cold was first recognized as a distinct medical condition by Benjamin Franklin in the 18th century. There is no formal classification system for acute viral nasopharyngitis. The pathophysiology involves the transmission of rhinoviruses, often through aerosols generated by coughing or sneezing. The virus typically enters the body through the nasal passages or lacrimal ducts, subsequently infecting epithelial cells. This triggers the release of inflammatory cytokines, which are responsible for the characteristic symptoms. The immune response involves both cellular and humoral mechanisms, with the body’s bacterial flora also playing a role in defense. The most common cause of acute viral nasopharyngitis is rhinovirus infection, though other viruses such as coronaviruses, human parainfluenza viruses, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) can also be implicated. It is important to differentiate the common cold from other conditions with overlapping symptoms, such as influenza, allergic rhinitis, and acute sinusitis. Epidemiologically, the common cold is the most prevalent human infection worldwide, accounting for approximately half of all visits to family physicians. Adults typically experience 2-3 episodes per year, while children may have 6-10 episodes annually. Among every 1,000 visits to family physicians, 500 are attributed to acute viral nasopharyngitis. Males are slightly more affected than females, and Native Americans are at higher risk for complications. Risk factors include close contact with infected individuals, attendance at daycare centers, allergic rhinitis, and immunocompromised states. The natural course of the common cold is self-limiting, with most cases resolving within 7-10 days. Complications, though uncommon, may include sinusitis, otitis media, and exacerbation of reactive airway diseases. Prognosis is excellent, with 50% of patients recovering within 7 days and 90% recovering within 15 days. The clinical presentation of acute viral nasopharyngitis includes symptoms such as a runny nose, cough, and sore throat. On physical examination, patients may appear unwell, with findings such as a runny nose, hyperemic nasal mucosa, and mild cervical lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests may reveal positive viral cultures, positive polymerase chain reaction (PCR) results, or leukocytosis on a complete blood count (CBC). However, imaging studies such as X-rays, CT scans, MRIs, or ultrasounds do not provide diagnostic value for this condition. Management of the common cold is primarily symptomatic. Analgesics, nasal decongestants, and cough suppressants may help alleviate symptoms. Antibiotics are not effective, as the condition is viral in origin, and no antiviral drugs have been approved for treatment. Despite popular beliefs, megadoses of vitamin C, zinc supplementation, and steam inhalation have not been proven to provide significant benefits. Surgical intervention is not indicated for the management of acute viral nasopharyngitis. These include avoiding close contact with infected individuals and practicing regular hand hygiene.
